doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

chapter: Personal life and the future of jazz
title: Does jazz have a future, and jazz education
summary: Moore is pessimistic about audiences and criticizes schools for teaching chords and scales instead of songs; he proposes a school for the American popular song.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: So you think the future of jazz — it still has a future?

My feeling is everybody says at these jazz parties everybody’s white haired in the audience and everything, and do you think there’s a future, and I say well I think if we’re lucky we’ll all die off at the same time. And it will all go with the audience. But then Harry says well thanks a lot. And I actually sometimes, I don’t know, I mean people say that but I’m glad I’m at the age I am. I don’t think I’d want to be 25 and liking the music

that I like and trying to make a living at it. I’m a pessimist enough to think that if Frank Sinatra were starting out singing now, he’d have a hell of a time getting a job, because of the climate of the times and the kind of music that’s popular. So I don’t know. All I know is I’m 52 and maybe I could eke out a living for another 25 years. But I mean certainly it’s going on in the schools, which I think there’s a pro and con to that. I think that like classical music, when it got institutionalized, I don’t think it was healthy for the music. But it got to the point where classical players only read notes off a page. But Mozart and Beethoven and up through Chopin, were all improvisers, they all would scare you to death. They’d throw each other themes and improvise on it. And I think now in jazz education a lot of that is happening in schools, where they have The Real Book, they have a set of chords and scales. And it’s very much more of an institutionalized thing. And that’s why I think it’s important that guys like Harry, who are song players, that kind of thing is not being taught in the colleges. And so I think that’s the important thread that’s going through, is the Harry Allens and the Ken Peplowskis, and a lot of them coming out of music school, they don’t know any songs. They can play their instruments and any chord, they can play a scale that goes with any chord, and play their originals or somebody else’s originals, that are set up for these improvisations. But there’s not the connection to the melody, and the love of the melody, and the great songs. In fact I have a student who is a young guitarist who is from this whole system that I was telling you about in college. He graduated. He plays great. I mean he plays the guitar beautifully. He plays beautiful solos and everything. And he’s coming to me for lessons, to teach him songs, because he doesn’t know any songs. And I say, “Well play a four bar intro” to something. He doesn’t know how to play a four bar introduction. Well what do I do? It seems like that’s the kind of thing that happens in schools. But when you come up playing on the street or playing in clubs, that’s the kind of thing you want to learn when you’re very young. In fact I was talking to Howard about it. I had an idea that that would be a good kind of school to start. It would be the American popular song and this kind of thing, and teach that.

It sounds like a great idea and to have people teaching that are professional players. Because I think sometimes the students are being taught by teachers who have just been teachers. And that they are great players themselves, but as you say, they might not know the songs enough themselves that they can pass it on. I guess there’s less venues to play and sometimes I think we don’t need more players, we need more audience.
